name: LifeWire ChromaDepth Spectral Vision Mod
body_location: retinal — bilateral photoreceptor surface coating with optic nerve signal bridge
description:
The ChromaDepth is a retinal surface implant applied bilaterally via ophthalmic micro-injection, depositing a structured photonic lattice across the cone-dense region of each retina. This lattice contains engineered photoreceptor analogs tuned to wavelength ranges beyond standard human trichromatic vision — specifically, a near-ultraviolet band (approximately 320-380nm) and an extended near-infrared band (approximately 750-850nm), effectively expanding the user's visible spectrum from the standard ~380-700nm range to a perceivable ~320-850nm window. The optic nerve signal bridge, a hairline filament seated at the posterior orbit, translates the novel photoreceptor signals into formats the visual cortex can learn to interpret — a process that takes 4-8 weeks of neuroplastic adaptation. During this period, LifeWire provides guided perceptual training via their ChromaDepth Calibrate app, using structured visual exercises that help the brain build new color categories for the expanded input. The result is genuine tetrachromatic-plus vision: users don't see ultraviolet and infrared as alien overlays but as new colors with no names in any existing language, integrated naturally into their full visual field.

The ChromaDepth attracts a wide and genuinely diverse user base that reflects how differently people value expanded perception. Visual artists — painters, textile designers, tattoo artists, fabricators working with dye lots — report that the implant fundamentally changes their professional capabilities, revealing undertones, fading patterns, and material inconsistencies invisible to unmodified eyes. Botanists, horticulturalists, and urban farmers use it to read plant health through UV-reflective stress markers on foliage. A significant recreational user base simply finds the expanded world beautiful: sunlight on water, the UV patterns on flowers that insects have always seen, the faint infrared warmth signatures of living things at dusk. For many users, the adaptation period — those weeks when the brain is slowly learning to see new colors — is described as one of the most disorienting and profound experiences of their lives, and ChromaDepth discussion forums are full of attempts to name the new colors, a shared creative project that has no resolution and no end.
installation_requirements: Licensed ophthalmic clinic; bilateral micro-injection procedure under topical anesthetic, approximately 35 minutes; 4-8 week neuroplastic adaptation period with guided training app
maintenance: Annual ophthalmic check to assess lattice integrity; photonic lattice rated for 12-year service life; app-guided recalibration if visual artifacts develop

side_effects: Significant visual disorientation during the 4-8 week adaptation period — new color signals perceived as flicker, shimmer, or visual noise before the brain learns to integrate them
Photosensitivity to UV-rich environments (direct sunlight, certain commercial lighting) until adaptation completes; ChromaDepth-rated eyewear recommended

Some users report that bright artificial lighting feels 'thin' or 'colorless' post-adaptation, as it lacks the UV and NIR content of natural light — a perceptual shift that can affect mood in low-quality lighting environments
Rare cases of persistent visual 'halo' around high-UV sources (certain screen types, UV sanitization lamps) that does not fully resolve with calibration
cultural_context: The ChromaDepth occupies a prestigious but not rarefied space in Meridian 88's implant culture — it is aspirational enough to carry a certain cachet but accessible enough that Tier 2 residents with strong motivation can save for it. Among artists and designers, having 'chroma eyes' is a professional credential as much as a personal choice, and some studios specifically seek out staff with spectral vision for color-critical work. There is a rich informal culture around the adaptation period: first-time ChromaDepth users are often guided through their weeks of visual adjustment by friends or online communities who share their own adaptation journals, attempts to name new colors, and the specific moment — different for everyone — when a new color suddenly becomes a color rather than visual static. That moment is called 'the click' in ChromaDepth communities, and people describe it with a reverence usually reserved for significant life events. Among Tier 4 and 5 users, paired ChromaDepth vision and ChromaDepth-aware interior design (spaces with deliberate UV and NIR elements invisible to baseline humans) has become a quiet status marker — a world within the world, visible only to those who've paid to see it.

Recreational users who simply want to experience the world with expanded beauty
Interior designers and architects working with ChromaDepth-aware spatial design
story_hooks: A character with ChromaDepth vision notices that a particular corporate logo — printed on packaging, building signage, and staff uniforms throughout a Tier 3 district — contains a UV-band glyph invisible to baseline humans, one that appears to be a structured symbol rather than a printing artifact. No one at the Corponation will confirm or deny what it means.

During the adaptation period, a new ChromaDepth user begins seeing what they believe is visual noise in a specific pattern — until they realize the 'noise' is a repeating structured signal embedded in the UV output of the city's standard streetlight grid, city-wide, broadcasting something to anyone with eyes to see it.

A renowned artist famous for ChromaDepth-only works — paintings that appear to be blank white canvases to unmodified eyes — is found dead, and the only witnesses are other ChromaDepth users who describe seeing something in the paintings that shouldn't have been there.
